owner.summary: Marisol is an independent software developer based in a small coastal town who maintains five unrelated side and client projects. She delegates routine coding, review and ops work to several AI coding agents that all read and write one shared memory server.

projects.summary: A payments service that handles merchant invoicing, settlement batches and refunds for small marine businesses. It keeps a double-entry ledger and reconciles against bank files each night. Idempotency and audit trails are the main design concerns.

A mobile app that lets hikers download offline trail maps, log walks and share routes with friends. It focuses on battery-efficient GPS tracking and fast tile rendering. The app is in beta with a few thousand testers.

A data pipeline that ingests sensor readings from regional grain silos and produces daily quality and moisture reports. It runs batch transforms and flags anomalies for operators. Backfills and schema drift are recurring headaches.
projects.stack: Python, message-stream broker, dbt, ClickHouse, workflow scheduler

projects.summary: A dedicated game server for a cooperative dungeon-crawler with up to eight players per session. It handles matchmaking, authoritative state and tick-based simulation. Current work targets lag compensation and reducing tick spikes.

A developer tool that lints infrastructure config files and suggests fixes with inline explanations. It ships as a single-binary command line tool with a plugin system for custom rules. Adoption is growing through a small open-source community.
projects.stack: TypeScript, Node, esbuild, WASM rules engine, CI runners

content: Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven decided on 8 June 2026 that every ledger_entry write in tidewallet-ledger carries a client-supplied idempotency_key stored in a unique index on the entries table, instead of deduplicating in Redis. Reason: a Redis eviction or failover would silently allow a duplicate posting, while the PostgreSQL constraint on pg-tide-primary cannot lapse. Redis-only dedupe lost.

On 15 June 2026 Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven chose gRPC with protobuf for all calls between ledger-api-01 and settle-worker-02, and rejected a REST/JSON internal API. Reason: the shared .proto files give one typed contract for settlement_batch and refund messages, and generated Go clients remove hand-written payload structs. Revisit only if a non-Go consumer needs the service.

Trap: running reconcile_nightly twice against the same bank file produced duplicate adjustment ledger_entry rows on 22 June 2026 because the job keyed adjustments on the run timestamp. The merchant_ledger drifted by 41 entries until they were reversed by hand. Key adjustments on the bank file name plus line number as the idempotency_key, so a rerun is a no-op.

settle-worker-02 runs the settlement worker as the systemd unit settle-worker.service, exposing gRPC on port 9443 and a health endpoint on port 8081. It was moved from a manual binary copy to a Terraform-managed instance with deploys through the make deploy-settle target on 2 July 2026. Logs go to /var/log/tidewallet/settle-worker.log.

Standing rule from Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven, stated 10 June 2026: no code path may update or delete a ledger_entry row. Corrections are made only by posting a new reversing entry that references the original entry id, so the double_entry trail stays intact for Odalys Brennick's compliance reviews. Migrations that touch the entries table must be reviewed by her before merge. Any helper, script or admin tool that issues UPDATE or DELETE against ledger_entry is rejected in code review, including one-off backfills. Backfills are written as insert-only migrations with a reason column filled in. The database role used by ledger-api-01 has no UPDATE or DELETE grant on that table, and this grant must not be widened for convenience. The rule reverses only if compliance changes the audit retention policy in writing.

Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven stated on 18 June 2026 that money amounts are always stored as int64 minor units with a separate currency code column, never as float or decimal strings in Go structs. Conversions to display format happen only at the API edge.

Status as of 20 August 2026, branch feat/refund-window. Landed: internal/refund/window.go computes the refund_window from the original settlement date (default 30 days, per-merchant override read from merchant_ledger config); internal/refund/service.go posts the reversing double_entry pair under one idempotency_key; proto/refund/v1/refund.proto is locked at v1 with RefundRequest, RefundResponse and the REFUND_WINDOW_CLOSED error code; migration db/migrations/0042_refund_window.sql adds refund_window_days to the merchants table. Tests in internal/refund/window_test.go cover leap day and timezone edges. Stubbed: chargeback interaction in internal/refund/chargeback.go returns ErrNotImplemented, so a refund on a disputed invoice is rejected for now. Stubbed: the dead_letter_queue retry for failed refund postings only logs and does not requeue. Not started: the merchant-facing webhook for refund status. Fenwick Aarav owns the chargeback stub follow-up. The proto must not change without bumping to v2, because settle-worker-02 already builds against v1.

Research finding on the pgx PostgreSQL driver for Go, checked 12 July 2026 at https://github.com/jackc/pgx. pgx v5 supports pgxpool with per-connection health checks, native binary protocol encoding for int64 and timestamptz, and CopyFrom for bulk inserts. The README and the pgxpool docs state that CopyFrom uses the COPY protocol, which cannot use ON CONFLICT clauses. That matters here because bulk loading bank file lines for reconcile_nightly would bypass the idempotency_key unique index handling. A duplicate in the batch aborts the whole COPY. Workable pattern: CopyFrom into a temporary staging table, then run INSERT ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING into the real table inside one transaction. Measured on pg-tide-primary with a 50,000 line sample file, the staging approach took about 1.4 seconds versus about 19 seconds for row-by-row inserts. pgxpool also needs MaxConns set below the PostgreSQL max_connections divided by the number of services, and the pool defaults to the larger of 4 or the CPU count, which is too low for settle-worker-02 under batch load.

Convention: every gRPC handler in ledger-api-01 reads the idempotency_key from the request metadata header x-idempotency-key and rejects the call with InvalidArgument if it is missing. Handlers never generate a key on the caller's behalf. Applies to all mutating RPCs from 1 July 2026.

Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven decided on 29 June 2026 to run settlement_batch jobs with a fixed payout_cutoff of 16:00 UTC, not a per-merchant local-time cutoff. Reason: one cutoff keeps the batch deterministic and simple to audit against the bank file. Per-merchant cutoffs lost because they multiplied batch runs and complicated reconciliation. Reverses if merchants outside the Atlantic and Pacific regions are onboarded.

Trap: Redis locks that guard settlement_batch runs expired mid-run on 5 August 2026 and a second settle-worker process started the same batch. Evidence: two log lines in /var/log/tidewallet/settle-worker.log showing batch 2026-08-05-A started at 16:00:02 and again at 16:00:34 on settle-worker-02. The lock was created with a fixed 30 second TTL, and a large batch of about 9,000 invoices ran longer than that, so the lock lapsed. The idempotency_key unique index stopped duplicate ledger_entry rows, so no money moved twice, but the second run filled the dead_letter_queue with 212 constraint-violation messages and the on-call alert fired. What to do instead: renew the lock on a heartbeat every 10 seconds while the batch is running and stop the batch if the renewal fails. Also add a PostgreSQL advisory lock (pg_try_advisory_lock keyed on the batch id) as the authoritative guard, and treat Redis only as a fast pre-check. Never rely on TTL length alone, since batch size grows with merchants. After a lock loss, drain the dead_letter_queue by checking that each failed message has a matching committed ledger_entry before discarding it.

Trap: Terraform plan for the ledger-api-01 security group showed no diff on 14 July 2026 although port 9443 had been opened by hand in the console. The state file had drifted, so apply later closed the port and settle-worker-02 calls failed for 11 minutes. Do not open ports by hand. Add the rule in the Terraform module, run plan, then apply.

Standing rule from Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven, stated 25 June 2026, on changes that touch money movement: every pull request that alters posting, settlement_batch, refund or chargeback code must include a test that replays the same request twice with one idempotency_key and asserts a single ledger_entry pair. The PR description must list which tables the change writes to. Odalys Brennick is added as reviewer on any PR that changes audit-trail columns or retention. Fenwick Aarav's contractor PRs follow the same rule and are not merged by the author. Merges to main need one approval from Marisol or a delegate she names in the PR thread. Hotfixes are the only exception to the second-reviewer wait, and even a hotfix keeps the replay test. If the replay test is slow, it is tagged integration and still runs in CI before merge. The rule has no expiry date.
Fenwick Aarav's contract tasks are limited to the settle-worker code, decided 1 July 2026, so ledger-api-01 posting code stays with the owner.
Redis docs on SET with NX and PX (https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/set/) say single-key locks are not safe across failover; Redlock needed for stronger guarantees.
Branch feat/dlq-replay, 9 September 2026: cmd/dlqreplay CLI landed for the dead_letter_queue; replay of refund messages is stubbed.

Trap: the nightly bank file from the acquirer began carrying a trailing summary line on 17 August 2026, and reconcile_nightly parsed it as a transaction with an empty reference. Evidence: the run on 18 August 2026 logged 1 unmatched line with amount 0 and the job exited non-zero, so the morning report to Odalys Brennick was missing. The parser in internal/reconcile/parse.go split on commas and accepted any row with at least four fields. Fix landed on 19 August 2026: rows whose first column is TRL are read as the trailer, and the control total and row count in it are checked against the parsed rows. Instead of loose field-count checks, validate the record type column explicitly and fail on unknown types. Also keep sample files for each bank format under testdata/bankfiles so a format change shows up as a failing test before the nightly run, not after it.
Go library golang-migrate (https://github.com/golang-migrate/migrate) runs each .sql file in one transaction only for some drivers; check the postgres driver notes before multi-statement files.
Log lines in all services use structured slog fields batch_id, merchant_id and idempotency_key; never log card or bank account numbers.

Status as of 2 October 2026 for the chargeback work, branch feat/chargeback-v1. Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven decided on 6 July 2026 that settlement_batch payouts to merchants are posted as one double_entry pair per merchant per batch, not one pair per invoice. Reason: it keeps the merchant_ledger readable and cuts ledger_entry volume. Per-invoice posting lost. Invoice-level detail stays in a batch_items table.

Trap: the Redis cache of merchant_ledger balances served stale values after a refund on 11 August 2026, and the merchant dashboard showed a balance 2,300 minor units too high for about nine minutes. Evidence: the ledger-api-01 log showed the refund ledger_entry committed at 14:02 UTC while the cache key merchant_ledger:balance:<merchant_id> kept its old value until its 600 second TTL ran out. The refund path wrote to PostgreSQL on pg-tide-primary but never touched the cache, because only the posting path had an invalidation call. Fenwick Aarav found it while comparing the dashboard with a direct SQL sum over ledger_entry. What to do instead: never treat the cache as a source of truth for money. Invalidate the balance key inside the same function that commits any ledger_entry, after the transaction commits and never before, so a failed commit does not drop a good value. Refunds, chargebacks and reversing entries all go through that function now. Any new write path must call it. Reconciliation and payout_cutoff checks read the balance directly from PostgreSQL with a SUM over ledger_entry, never from Redis. If a cache read is needed for display only, label the field as approximate in the API response.

Every migration file in db/migrations is named with a four digit sequence number and a snake_case description, for example 0043_batch_items.sql, and ships with a matching down file only if it creates a new table. Migrations that alter the entries table also need review by Odalys Brennick before merge.

pg-tide-primary runs PostgreSQL 16 on port 5432, reachable only from the private subnet that holds ledger-api-01 and settle-worker-02. Nightly base backups go to the object bucket defined in terraform/storage.tf, and WAL is archived continuously. Direct psql access for humans goes through the bastion only.

ledger-api-01 serves gRPC on port 9443 behind the internal load balancer and a health endpoint on port 8080. The Go binary deploys with make deploy ENV=prod, which builds the image, pushes it and restarts the systemd unit ledger-api.service. Terraform for the instance lives in terraform/ledger-api.tf.

Convention for error handling in all Go packages of tidewallet-ledger. Errors are wrapped with fmt.Errorf and the %w verb so callers can use errors.Is and errors.As. Sentinel errors live in the package that owns the concept, for example ErrRefundWindowClosed in internal/refund and ErrDuplicateKey in internal/ledger. gRPC handlers translate sentinel errors to status codes in one place, internal/grpcutil/errors.go, and never inline in the handler body. The mapping is: ErrDuplicateKey returns the stored result of the original call with status OK, not an error, because idempotency_key replays must look identical to the first call. Validation failures return InvalidArgument. A missing merchant returns NotFound. A closed refund_window returns FailedPrecondition with the detail code REFUND_WINDOW_CLOSED. Any database error that is not a known constraint violation returns Internal and the original error is logged with batch_id, merchant_id and idempotency_key as slog fields, but its text is never sent to the caller. Panics are recovered by an interceptor that logs the stack and returns Internal. Code that swallows an error with _ = is rejected in review unless a comment names the reason. Messages sent to the dead_letter_queue keep the original error string in a separate column so replay tooling can group failures. Reverses only if the error contract in the shared .proto files is revised and bumped to a new version.
Trap: go test ran against pg-tide-primary on 3 August 2026 and wrote fixture rows. Tests must use the local docker PostgreSQL only.

Trap: settle-worker-02 retried a failed settlement_batch on 26 July 2026 using a fresh idempotency_key each attempt, so two payout postings of 9,400 minor units reached the merchant_ledger. Evidence: two ledger_entry rows with different keys and the same batch_id. Instead, derive the key from batch_id and merchant_id so every retry reuses it.

Decision by Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven on 14 September 2026, replacing the earlier note that only said golang-migrate runs each .sql file in one transaction for some drivers and to check the postgres driver notes. The team now wraps every migration file in an explicit BEGIN and COMMIT, and golang-migrate is run with the postgres driver option x-multi-statement=false so it sends each file as a single simple-protocol exec rather than splitting statements. Reason: on 9 September 2026 a staging migration 0044_batch_items.sql failed halfway, left the table created without its unique index on (batch_id, merchant_id), and the next run errored with relation already exists. Explicit transactions make the file all or nothing because PostgreSQL DDL is transactional. Exceptions: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction, so those statements live alone in a file named with the suffix _concurrent.sql, are written to be re-runnable with IF NOT EXISTS, and must be reviewed by hand before applying to pg-tide-primary. Alternative that lost: relying on the driver's default behavior per version, rejected because the behavior differs between driver releases and cannot be checked from the file alone. Alternative that also lost: a custom migration runner, rejected as more code to audit. Reverses if golang-migrate documents a guaranteed per-file transaction for the postgres driver, in which case the explicit BEGIN and COMMIT can be dropped.

Standing rule from Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven, stated 27 July 2026, on reviews of anything that changes what a merchant is paid. A pull request that changes payout amounts, fees, rounding or the payout_cutoff must carry a worked example in its description with real minor-unit numbers, for instance an invoice of 10,000 with a 2.9 percent fee yielding a fee of 290 and a payout of 9,710. Odalys Brennick is tagged on the pull request for compliance review, and the change is not merged until she has commented. Measurement from the reconcile_nightly run on settle-worker-02 against the acquirer bank file of 24 August 2026: 18,420 transaction lines parsed and matched to ledger_entry rows in 41 seconds, peak resident memory 212 MB. Matching used the batch_id and reference index on pg-tide-primary. The same file before the index was added on 20 August 2026 took 3 minutes 52 seconds. Source: the run summary line in /var/log/tidewallet/settle-worker.log.

Standing rule from Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven, stated 3 September 2026, on database migrations that touch the ledger. Any migration that alters the ledger_entry table or any table the double_entry posting path reads must be reviewed by Odalys Brennick before merge, and the pull request must say so in its description. The migration must be tested on a restored copy of a pg-tide-primary backup in the local docker PostgreSQL, never on pg-tide-primary itself. It must be additive: new nullable columns or new tables only, with no column rewrites that hold a lock longer than one second on that copy. Destructive changes such as dropping a column wait until a release after the code stopped reading it. Reverses only if compliance changes the review requirement in writing.
The idempotency_key lookup on ledger-api-01 took a median of 1.8 ms and a p99 of 6 ms over 50,000 posting calls on 12 September 2026.

PostgreSQL documentation on INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-insert.html) states that DO NOTHING skips a conflicting row without locking it and returns no row for it. For idempotency_key inserts, a follow-up SELECT is needed to read the stored result of the original call. Under concurrent inserts of the same key, one transaction waits for the other to commit or abort before deciding.

settle-worker-02 runs the settlement worker as the systemd unit tidewallet-settle.service, effective 18 August 2026. The binary sits at /opt/tidewallet/bin/settle-worker and reads its environment from /etc/tidewallet/settle-worker.env, which holds no secrets. Database and Redis credentials are fetched at start from the secret manager path named in terraform/secrets.tf. Logs go to /var/log/tidewallet/settle-worker.log and rotate daily with 14 files kept. The unit restarts on failure after 10 seconds, with a limit of 5 restarts in 5 minutes before it stays down and pages. Deploys use make deploy ENV=prod TARGET=settle-worker, which builds the image, copies the binary and restarts the unit. The worker listens on port 8081 for a health endpoint only, reachable from the private subnet. It runs reconcile_nightly at 02:00 UTC and settlement_batch runs after that, before the payout_cutoff.

Redis for tidewallet-ledger runs as a single managed instance defined in terraform/cache.tf, reachable only from the private subnet that holds ledger-api-01 and settle-worker-02, on port 6379 with TLS. It holds three kinds of data: settlement_batch run locks with a 120 second TTL, cached merchant_ledger balances with a 60 second TTL, and rate-limit counters. Nothing in Redis is a source of truth, so a full flush is safe and only costs a cold cache. Persistence is off. The dead_letter_queue is not in Redis and lives in PostgreSQL on pg-tide-primary. Humans reach Redis only through the bastion. Changes to the instance size or eviction policy go through Terraform in CI. The eviction policy is allkeys-lru with a 1 GB memory limit, and lock keys are set with NX and PX so that an eviction cannot silently extend a lock.

Measurement from a settlement_batch dry run on settle-worker-02 on 9 September 2026 against a copy of August data: 1,260 merchants and 31,800 invoices produced 1,260 double_entry pairs, so 2,520 ledger_entry rows, in 3 minutes 14 seconds. Posting ran in transactions of 50 merchants, and the peak lock wait on pg-tide-primary was 140 ms. Per-invoice posting on the same data would have written 63,600 ledger_entry rows.
The Terraform state for tidewallet-ledger lives in the remote backend configured in terraform/backend.tf, with locking on, since 2 July 2026.

Every gRPC handler in ledger-api-01 that mutates money requires an idempotency_key in the request metadata and returns the code InvalidArgument when it is missing. The handler stores the key and the response in one transaction with the ledger_entry rows, so a replay returns the stored response and posts nothing. Keys are scoped per merchant_id and kept for 90 days. New mutating RPCs copy this pattern from internal/api/interceptors/idempotency.go instead of writing their own check.
Money amounts are int64 minor units with a separate three letter currency code field; no float type appears in any amount path.

Odalys Brennick is the compliance reviewer for tidewallet-ledger. She reviews every migration that touches the entries tables and signs off on changes to audit trail fields and on how long records are kept. She prefers written review requests that list the affected tables and link the pull request, and she answers in the pull request thread, not in chat. She does not write code in the repository. Questions about whether a field may be logged or stored go to her before implementation starts.

Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven decided on 21 July 2026 that the refund_window is 120 days from the original settlement_batch posting date. Reason: the acquirer accepts chargebacks for up to 120 days, so a shorter window would let merchants refund less than the card holder can dispute. A 90 day window lost because it left a gap of 30 days. Refunds after the window are rejected with a typed error and handled manually. Reverses if the acquirer contract changes its dispute period.

Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven decided on 28 September 2026 that settlement_batch payouts are posted as one double_entry pair per merchant per payout_cutoff window, replacing the 6 July 2026 decision that posted one pair per merchant per batch. Reason: merchants with two batches in one cutoff window, which happened for 37 merchants in the 9 September 2026 dry run, saw two payout lines for a single bank transfer, and the bank file matched one transfer to two ledger pairs during reconcile_nightly. The new rule posts one pair per merchant per cutoff window and records the contributing batch ids in batch_items. Per-invoice posting stays rejected. Invoice-level detail remains in batch_items, and the merchant_ledger view groups by cutoff window. Reverses if the acquirer starts sending one transfer per batch. Reference for the grouping approach: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-GROUP. The earlier decision no longer applies.

The state had drifted, so the next apply closed the port and settle-worker-02 calls failed for 12 minutes. Never open ports by hand. Add the rule in the Terraform module, run plan in CI, then apply.

pg-tide-primary runs PostgreSQL 16 on port 5432 and accepts connections only from the private subnet holding ledger-api-01 and settle-worker-02. Nightly base backups go to the bucket declared in terraform/storage.tf and WAL is archived continuously. Humans reach psql through the bastion only, never directly. Branch feat/dlq-replay, 11 September 2026: the cmd/dlqreplay CLI landed for the dead_letter_queue and replays settlement_batch messages only. Files: cmd/dlqreplay/main.go holds the flag parsing, internal/dlq/replay.go holds the requeue logic, and internal/dlq/replay_test.go covers it against the local docker PostgreSQL. The flags are --kind, --since and --dry-run, and --dry-run prints the message ids without requeueing. Replay of refund messages is stubbed and returns an error saying the kind is not supported yet. Replayed messages keep their original idempotency_key so a second replay posts nothing. The CLI reads the database address from the environment and has no default, so it cannot reach pg-tide-primary by accident. It runs from settle-worker-02 through the bastion only, and the binary is built by make build-dlqreplay into bin/dlqreplay. Nothing from this branch is deployed to production yet.

Trap: the nightly job on settle-worker-02 failed on 29 August 2026 because the bank file arrived at 02:40 UTC, after reconcile_nightly had started at 02:00 and found no file. Evidence: the log showed 'no input file' and zero rows reconciled, and the next run flagged 9,100 unmatched minor units per merchant average. Instead, the job waits for the file with a 90 minute timeout and pages if it is absent, and the file name is checked against the date.
Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven decided on 2 August 2026 to keep the dead_letter_queue in PostgreSQL, not in Redis, so failed messages survive a cache flush and restart.

Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven decided on 15 August 2026 that chargeback postings use a separate set of ledger accounts, chargeback_held and chargeback_lost, instead of reusing the refund accounts. Reason: a chargeback has two outcomes, resolved for the merchant or lost, and the funds must sit in a held account between the two so that the merchant_ledger available balance drops at the moment the acquirer reports it. Refund accounts were designed for merchant-initiated reversals inside the refund_window and have no held state. Research finding: PostgreSQL documents that session-level advisory locks are not released on transaction rollback and stay held until the session ends or pg_advisory_unlock is called, while transaction-level locks from pg_advisory_xact_lock release at commit or rollback. Source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/explicit-locking.html#ADVISORY-LOCKS. The page also says session locks follow the connection, so behind a pooler that reuses connections in transaction mode a session lock can outlive the work that took it or be released by a different client. For tidewallet-ledger this supports the xact variant for settlement_batch posting, since a crashed worker cannot leave a lock behind. The docs also state that advisory lock slots live in shared memory, sized by max_locks_per_transaction times max_connections, so a batch taking one lock per merchant must be checked against that limit on pg-tide-primary.

Research finding: the IETF HTTP API working group draft for the Idempotency-Key header, https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/, defines how a client sends a unique key with a non-idempotent request so a retry is safe. Key points that match the tidewallet-ledger design: the server stores the key together with the request, so a second request with the same key but a different payload is rejected with 422 instead of being replayed; a second request that arrives while the first is still running gets 409; and keys are expected to be scoped to the client, not global. The draft leaves the key lifetime to the server and says it should be published. Stripe's public API reference, https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests, shows the production version of the same idea. It saves the status code and body of the first request for a key, including failures, returns the saved result on a repeat, accepts keys up to 255 characters, and may remove keys after 24 hours. For tidewallet-ledger the useful points are the request hash comparison and the saved response, both of which are in internal/idempotency. The key lifetime is still open and needs input from Odalys Brennick because audit retention is longer than 24 hours.

Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven decided on 22 July 2026 that settlement_batch runs are retried at most 5 times with exponential backoff, and after that the message goes to the dead_letter_queue table on pg-tide-primary and is never retried automatically again. Backoff starts at 30 seconds and doubles each attempt, with jitter of up to 20 percent, so the waits are about 30, 60, 120, 240 and 480 seconds. Reason: settlement failures are mostly a bank file problem, a lock conflict or a database failover. The first two clear within minutes and the third within the backoff span. A failure beyond that needs a person, and unlimited retries risk hiding it while the payout_cutoff passes. A bounded count also keeps the audit trail readable, since each attempt writes one audit record with the attempt number and error text. Lost: unlimited retries with a ceiling on delay, which Fenwick Aarav proposed because it needs no manual replay. It lost because it would delay a stuck batch past payout_cutoff without anyone noticing. Also lost: a fixed 3 attempts, which failed the 19 June 2026 failover test where the database was unavailable for 4 minutes. Replay from the dead_letter_queue is manual through cmd/dlqreplay with --dry-run first. Reverses if the dead_letter_queue grows past 50 messages a week for 3 weeks, at which point the retry count and backoff are reviewed.

Research finding: the pgxpool package documentation at https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool lists the pool settings that matter for tidewallet-ledger. MaxConns defaults to the larger of 4 and the CPU count, so a worker on a small host gets a very small pool unless it is set. MinConns defaults to 0. MaxConnLifetime defaults to one hour and MaxConnIdleTime to 30 minutes, and HealthCheckPeriod defaults to one minute. The pool is built with pgxpool.ParseConfig, which also reads pool_max_conns and similar keys from the connection string, so a limit can be changed without a code edit. The package states that Acquire returns a connection that must be released, and that a connection held through a transaction is not returned until commit or rollback. That bears on settle-worker-02, where a settlement_batch worker holding a connection while waiting on a gRPC call keeps a slot busy. Practical consequences: set MaxConns explicitly in both ledger-api-01 and settle-worker-02 so their sum stays under the max_connections value on pg-tide-primary, never hold a connection across a network call, and run the idempotency lookup and the double_entry insert in one transaction on one acquired connection.

Convention for posting money in tidewallet-ledger: all writes to ledger_entry go through internal/ledger.Post and nowhere else. Post opens one pgx transaction and inserts the idempotency_key row first; a unique violation there means the request was already applied, and Post returns the stored result without posting again. It then inserts every ledger_entry of the transaction and asserts that debits equal credits per currency before commit, with the same rule enforced by a deferred constraint trigger in PostgreSQL so a bug in Go cannot bypass it. There is no UPDATE or DELETE on ledger_entry in application code; a correction is a new reversing pair that references the original entry id. Amounts are int64 minor units. Each handler maps Post errors to gRPC codes: AlreadyExists is never returned for a replayed key, because a replay returns the original success; FailedPrecondition is used for a closed refund_window; Aborted is used for serialization failures, which the caller may retry with the same key. A new code path that writes ledger_entry needs a test in internal/testdb style that checks the double_entry sum is zero at the end. Reason for all of it: one write path makes the audit trail and the idempotency guarantee reviewable in one file.

Research finding: the PostgreSQL 16 documentation on transaction isolation, https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/transaction-iso.html, states that applications using Repeatable Read or Serializable must be prepared to retry transactions that fail with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure), and that the retry must run the whole transaction again, not only the failed statement. At Read Committed, which is the default, each statement sees a fresh snapshot, so two concurrent transactions can both read the same balance and both pass a check that is applied in Go code. The same page says that Serializable mode uses predicate locks that do not block, and that long-running read-write transactions raise the chance of failures. Relevance to tidewallet-ledger: any balance check that must hold across concurrent refunds on one merchant_ledger either runs at Serializable inside a retry loop, or takes a row lock with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the merchant balance row. Relevant error handling in pgx is to read pgconn.PgError and compare Code to 40001 before retrying. The retry loop should be bounded and should reuse the same idempotency_key, so a retry after an ambiguous commit does not post twice.

Research finding: the Redis documentation on distributed locks, https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use/patterns/distributed-locks/, describes the single-instance pattern as SET key random_value NX PX ttl, released by a Lua script that deletes the key only if the stored value still matches. The random value stops a client whose lock expired from deleting a lock now held by another client. For tidewallet-ledger this means lock keys in the 2 GB Redis instance carry a per-holder random value and a TTL longer than the longest settlement_batch page.

Research finding: the pgx documentation, https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jackc/pgx/v5, describes pgx.BeginTx with TxOptions that set IsoLevel, and pgconn.PgError exposes a Code field that carries the SQLSTATE. Unique violation is 23505 and serialization failure is 40001. The pgxpool package manages a pool of connections, with MaxConns defaulting to the larger of 4 or the number of CPUs. Batch support through pgx.Batch sends several queries in one round trip. For tidewallet-ledger this means internal/ledger.Post can detect a repeated idempotency_key by checking for code 23505 on the idempotency_key insert, and can retry the whole transaction on 40001. The default MaxConns is low for ledger-api-01 under load, so it must be set explicitly in the pool config. The documentation does not promise any retry behavior, so the retry loop has to live in our code with a bounded attempt count.

Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven decided on 18 August 2026 that settlement_batch payouts are built in two phases, a freeze phase and a send phase, and not in one pass. In the freeze phase, tidewallet-settle.service selects all ledger_entry rows for each merchant_ledger up to the 16:00 UTC payout_cutoff, writes them into settlement_batch items inside one transaction, and marks the batch frozen with the sum per merchant. In the send phase, a separate step reads only frozen batches and submits them to the bank, with the batch id used as the idempotency_key for the bank call. Reason: a crash during sending then never changes which entries belong to a batch, a retry sends the same batch with the same key, and the audit trail shows exactly what was frozen and when. Odalys Brennick asked for that separation so a reviewer can compare the frozen sum with the bank confirmation. The single-pass design lost because a crash halfway through left no record of which entries had been included, and recomputing after the crash could pick up late entries and pay a different amount under the same batch. A design that held a database lock during the whole bank call also lost, because bank calls took up to 40 seconds and blocked posting from ledger-api-01. Reverses only if the bank offers an atomic batch API that accepts the freeze and send as one operation with its own idempotency, and Marisol agrees the audit trail still shows the frozen sum.

Layout of the nightly reconcile pipeline on settle-worker-02, as of 3 October 2026. A systemd timer, tidewallet-reconcile.timer, starts tidewallet-reconcile.service at 02:30 UTC every day. The service runs /opt/tidewallet/bin/settle-worker reconcile and reads its environment from /etc/tidewallet/settle.env, which holds only references to secrets and never the secrets themselves. The input is the newest file in /var/lib/tidewallet/bank-files/incoming, delivered by SFTP from the acquirer. After a run the file is moved to /var/lib/tidewallet/bank-files/processed with the run date in its name, or to /var/lib/tidewallet/bank-files/failed if parsing stops. The job connects to pg-tide-primary on port 5432 with the reconcile role, which can read ledger_entry and write only to unmatched_bank_row and the reconcile_run table. Matched rows are recorded by writing a link row in reconcile_match, never by changing the ledger_entry. Messages that fail validation go to the dead_letter_queue in Redis, capped at 10000 with an alert at 5000. Logs go to journald under the unit name and are shipped to the central log store with a 90 day retention. A run that finds rows unmatched for three nights adds them to the weekly list that Odalys Brennick reviews. The timer has Persistent=true, so a run missed during downtime starts at boot.

Trap: the migration that added the refund_of column to ledger_entry on 29 September 2026 ran on staging in 3 seconds, but the same migration on a production-sized copy of pg-tide-primary held an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for 4 minutes and blocked ledger-api-01 postings. The cause was adding the column together with a NOT NULL default and a new index in one statement, which rewrote the table and built the index under the lock. Evidence: pg_stat_activity showed postings waiting on the migration session, and gRPC calls timed out at the 5 second deadline. What to do instead: add the column as nullable, backfill in batches of 5000 rows, add the constraint as NOT VALID and validate it later, and build the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in a separate migration file. Test every ledger_entry migration on the production-sized copy before Odalys Brennick reviews it, and set lock_timeout to 3 seconds in the migration session so it fails fast.

Research finding on pgx for the Go database layer in tidewallet-ledger. The pgx documentation describes pgx.Tx as supporting nested transactions through savepoints when Begin is called on an existing transaction, and says Rollback after Commit returns pgx.ErrTxClosed, which is safe to ignore in a deferred call. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jackc/pgx/v5. This supports the rule that callers own begin, commit and rollback, with a deferred Rollback right after Begin. The same page notes that pgxpool.Pool must be closed on shutdown to release connections, so ledger-api-01 and settle-worker-02 both call pool.Close in their signal handlers. It also documents that a batch queued through pgx.Batch runs in a single round trip, which is a candidate for posting both sides of a double_entry pair, but the team has not adopted it, because error attribution per statement is harder to read in the audit trail.

Trap: a float64 crept into an amount path in tidewallet-ledger and cost a day of reconciliation debugging. On 15 September 2026 a payout summary helper in settle-worker-02 parsed a gRPC amount into float64 to compute a merchant fee share, and reconcile_nightly then reported a mismatch of 1 minor unit on 19 settlement_batch rows against the bank file, while the ledger_entry rows summed correctly. A fee share of 12499 EUR times 0.035 has no exact binary floating point value, and its rounding differed from the integer rounding used in the merchant_ledger. The rule is that money amounts are int64 minor units with a separate three letter currency code field, and no float type appears in any amount path, including helpers, reports and test fixtures. Do instead: compute shares with integer arithmetic, multiply first and divide last, round down to whole minor units and carry the remainder in the merchant_ledger. To find a leak, grep the Go tree for float64 and float32 near amount, fee and payout identifiers, and check that double_entry debits equal credits in the test covering the helper. Reverses only if the acquirer interface requires decimal strings, and even then the conversion happens at the edge, not in the ledger.

Working rule for the dead_letter_queue in tidewallet-ledger: a message moves to the dead_letter_queue after 5 failed delivery attempts and keeps its original idempotency_key, payload and the error text of the last attempt. Replays are done only through the replay command, which resubmits the message under the same idempotency_key, so a message that already posted returns the stored result and does not post a second ledger_entry pair. The payload of a queued message is never edited by hand. If a payload is wrong, the message is closed with a reason and a corrected request is submitted under a new idempotency_key, so the audit trail shows both. Any message that stays in the dead_letter_queue for more than 3 days is listed in the morning check of settle-worker-02 and is reviewed by Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven or her delegate. Messages for refunds or chargebacks are not replayed after the refund_window has closed, and are closed with that reason instead.

SQLite documentation states that WAL mode lets readers and one writer proceed concurrently, but it does not work over network filesystems. Fernpath-trails confirmed on 5 July 2026 that the fernpath-api sync.db sits on local disk, so WAL is enabled with PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL and PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL. The documentation also describes checkpoint starvation, where long-running readers keep the WAL file from being reset, so export jobs on fernpath-api must close read transactions within 30 seconds. Source: https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html. Revisit if sync.db moves to a network volume.

Standing rule from Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven, set on 2 September 2026, replacing her 3 August 2026 decision to resolve sync_conflict by last-writer-wins per waypoint. The earlier rule is reversed because beta_channel testers who walk with a phone and a watch-linked tablet lost edited waypoint names and notes when the later device overwrote the whole waypoint. The new rule: sync_conflict is resolved by field-level merge per waypoint. Each waypoint field (name, note, latitude, longitude, elevation, icon) carries its own updated_at timestamp in milliseconds, and the server keeps the value with the newest timestamp for each field separately. Coordinates are treated as one field pair and always taken together from the same writer so a waypoint never ends up with a latitude from one device and a longitude from another. Deletions win only if the delete timestamp is newer than every field timestamp on the other side. Ties on updated_at go to the device with the lexicographically smaller device id so results are deterministic. Implementation lives in shared/src/commonMain/kotlin/sync/WaypointMerge.kt, and any change to it needs the migration test required by the 17 June 2026 rule when it touches stored columns. This reverses if the field timestamps cause more than 1 percent of syncs to produce a waypoint the user did not author, measured in the weekly feedback digest.

Research finding on MapLibre Native as the renderer option for fernpath-trails, read on 9 July 2026 from the MapLibre Native documentation at https://maplibre.org/maplibre-native/docs/book/. MapLibre Native is an open source fork of Mapbox GL Native from before its licence change, and it ships for Android (Kotlin and Java API) and iOS (Swift and Objective-C API) with the same style specification. It reads vector tiles in the Mapbox Vector Tile format and can load tiles from a local MBTiles file or from a custom URL scheme, which fits an offline_tile_pack stored on the device. The documentation describes an offline region API that downloads tiles for a bounding box and zoom range into an ambient cache, with a tile count limit set by the host application, so the cache is not a fixed pack file that can be shipped from a server. The same documentation states that GL rendering runs on a dedicated render thread and that style changes must be made on the main thread on Android. Conclusion recorded for the project: use MapLibre with MBTiles-style packs served from tiles-edge-eu and not its ambient cache, because pack files can be versioned, checksummed and resumed. Reverses if the offline region API gains named, downloadable pack archives.

Workflow scheduler convention on flowsched-main: every DAG file lives in dags/ and is named after its DAG id, for example dags/grainflow_daily.py holds grainflow_daily. Each task must be idempotent, because the scheduler retries failed tasks up to 3 times with a 5 minute delay. Tasks take their date from the scheduler logical date, never from datetime.now(), so that reruns and backfills reproduce the same output. Tasks that write to ClickHouse do so by replacing a whole partition, not by appending rows. Failure alerts go to the operators channel named grainflow-ops. Any new DAG needs a short entry in docs/dags.md listing its schedule, owner and upstream dependencies, and is paused on creation until that entry is reviewed.

ClickHouse documentation on partitioning states that partitions are intended as a data management tool, not a query speed-up, and recommends keeping the total count of partitions in the low hundreds because too many partitions slow inserts and merges, with a default limit of 1,000 partitions touched per insert block (max_partitions_per_insert_block, default 100 in recent releases). Relevance to grainflow-pipeline: the daily_rollup partition_key of (region_code, toYYYYMM(reading_date)) gives about 456 partitions per year, so a single insert that spans many regions and months can hit the per-insert limit. A 150 ms window covers the round-trip of 94% of observed players in EU and US shards, based on ember-metrics data from July 2026. Cassius Mbeki confirmed that enemy attack telegraphs last at least 400 ms, so a 150 ms window cannot let a player dodge an attack retroactively. Lost: a 250 ms window, which let high-ping players hit enemies that had already died on other screens. Reverses if the share of players covered falls under 90% or if desync reports about phantom kills rise.

Emberhold deployment layout as of September 2026. Four hosts: ember-match-01 runs the matchmaking Deployment with one replica, UDP 7770 for lobby_token handshakes and TCP 8080 for health. ember-shard-eu1 and ember-shard-us2 each run a StatefulSet named emberhold-shard with up to 12 pods, every pod exposing UDP 7780 for game traffic via hostPort and TCP 8081 for the readiness probe. Results of the 14 August 2026 lag_compensation load test on ember-shard-eu1, run in the staging namespace with 40 simulated sessions of 8 bots each, 320 clients total, for 30 minutes at tick_rate 30. Network shaping used tc netem with 60 ms delay, 20 ms jitter and 1% loss. Without lag_compensation, 23.4% of shots that hit on the client were rejected by the server. With a 150 ms rollback_window, rejected hits fell to 3.1%. A window of 100 ms gave 7.8% and a window of 250 ms gave 1.9%, but the 250 ms setting produced 412 phantom kills, where an enemy died on the server after already dying elsewhere, against 37 at 150 ms. Median tick time rose from 3.1 ms to 3.6 ms, p99 from 7.8 ms to 9.4 ms. The rewind buffer added 14 MB of memory per shard pod at 12 live sessions. These numbers came from the ember-metrics dashboard export saved as lagcomp-0814.csv in the team drive.

The tokio-metrics crate reports per-task poll duration and scheduled delay for Tokio runtimes. Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven decided on 17 September 2026 to keep the authoritative simulation on a dedicated thread per session instead of scheduling every session as a Tokio task. Reasons: the tick loop is CPU-bound and a single long tick on a shared worker delayed other sessions, which showed up as correlated spikes across sessions in the ember-metrics capture of 28 July 2026 on ember-shard-us2. A dedicated thread isolates one session's cost from the rest, and per-session thread affinity keeps the rollback_window ring buffer warm in cache. Tokio stays responsible for UDP receive and send and for the matchmaking handshake, and the two sides exchange messages over bounded channels with a capacity of 256. Lost: the single runtime design, which was simpler to reason about and needed no channel hop between network and simulation. Lost: a rayon pool for simulation work, because it would have mixed unrelated sessions on the same threads again. Cost: one thread per live session, up to about 40 per shard host at current capacity. Reverses if a shard hosts more than 100 concurrent sessions or if thread count causes scheduler contention measured in ember-metrics.
A hot reload of loot_table on 24 August 2026 stalled ticks for 90 ms on ember-shard-eu1. Do not reload tables on a live shard; roll the pods instead.

Raising tick_rate to 60 on ember-shard-us2 pushed p99 tick time beyond the 16.7 ms budget at that rate and was rolled back on 14 September 2026. Hold tick_rate at 30 on every shard until the loot_table cache lands, because loot parsing was the main source of spikes. Scope: the change was only tried on ember-shard-us2, and ember-shard-eu1 stayed at 30 throughout. The earlier 33.3 ms budget at tick_rate 30 is unaffected. Status note: the rollback was done by reverting the tick_rate value in the shard Deployment configuration and rolling the pods one at a time. No sessions were lost in the rollout because the pods were drained of new lobbies first. Retry condition: repeat the 60 trial only after the loot cache is live on main and a staging load test with 320 clients at tick_rate 60 shows p99 below 12 ms. The cache work is tracked in the loot cache pull request, and the 60 trial should use the same ember-metrics capture method as the 28 July 2026 profile so the numbers compare directly. Until that retest, client builds should keep assuming 30 ticks per second for interpolation, and no client code should depend on 60.

Convention for logging and tracing in emberhold-server, adopted 20 August 2026. All logs use the tracing crate with structured fields, never format strings with values baked in. Every log line inside a session carries the fields shard_id and session id, and lines about a player also carry party_slot. Lobby_token values are never logged in full: log only the first 6 characters. Levels: error for events that end a session, warn for recoverable desync or dropped packets above threshold, info for session start and end, debug for per-tick detail. Per-tick logging at debug level is compiled out of release builds with the tracing max_level_release_info feature, so it costs nothing in production. Do not log inside the tick loop at info level or above, because log writes caused measurable spikes in the 5 August 2026 profiling. Anything that must be reported per tick goes through the metrics counters in src/metrics.rs, which ember-metrics scrapes. Log output goes to stdout as JSON and the cluster collects it, so code must not write log files. When adding a new subsystem, create a tracing span named after the module and enter it at the top of the main function for that module. Reviewers check these rules on every pull request touching src/net/ or src/sim/.

Staging runs in the staging namespace on the same Kubernetes cluster as ember-shard-eu1. It has one matchmaking replica listening on UDP 7770 and two shard pods on UDP 7780, and it is the only place load tests may run. Deploy with kubectl apply -n staging -f deploy/staging/. It is reset nightly.

Emberhold shard pods on ember-shard-eu1 and ember-shard-us2 run as a Kubernetes StatefulSet named emberhold-shard in the production namespace. Each pod reads its configuration from the ConfigMap emberhold-shard-config, mounted at /etc/emberhold/shard.toml, which sets tick_rate, the shard_id prefix and the session_reaper interval. The game socket is UDP 7780 and the metrics endpoint is TCP 9100. terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 120, so a pod being replaced stops accepting new party_slot assignments and lets live sessions finish before it exits. Config changes need a pod roll because the file is read once at startup. Logs go to stdout as JSON and are collected by the cluster log agent.

Party_slot values are zero-indexed, 0 to 7, everywhere on the server: Rust code, the Protobuf schema, logs and metrics labels. Only the client UI shows slots as 1 to 8. Never add a +1 or -1 conversion in server code. Reject any pull request that does, because a mismatched slot assigns state to the wrong player and shows up as desync.

Idle players in a lobby were dropped by the network path because the UDP conntrack entry on the Kubernetes nodes expired after 30 seconds without traffic. Symptom: on 3 September 2026, 14 of 52 players waiting in lobbies on ember-match-01 stopped receiving lobby_token updates after sitting idle for about half a minute, and the matchmaker logged no error because UDP has no connection state to close. Players saw a frozen lobby and had to rejoin, which cost them their queue position. The first guess was a bug in the matchmaking Deployment, and two days went into reading handshake code on UDP 7770 that was correct. The cause was found only when a packet capture on the node showed the server replies leaving the pod but never reaching clients after the idle gap. What to do instead: have the matchmaker and clients send a keepalive datagram every 10 seconds while a lobby is open, well under the 30 second conntrack timeout, and treat 3 missed keepalives as a disconnect. Do not raise the node conntrack timeout, because that setting is shared with other workloads on the cluster. When lobby clients freeze with no server error, check the idle gap against the conntrack timeout before reading handshake code.
Loopback runs on ember-shard-eu1 show zero desync since loopback has no jitter or loss. Use tc netem: 60 ms delay, 20 ms jitter, 2% loss. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/tc-netem.8.html

Emberhold shard rollout procedure as of 22 September 2026. Releases come from main as an image tagged with the short git SHA, and the rollout targets the StatefulSet emberhold-shard with updateStrategy RollingUpdate and partition set to 1 first, so only the highest-numbered pod updates as a canary. The canary pod on ember-shard-eu1 is watched for 15 minutes on the ember-metrics Grafana tick time dashboard, and the rollout continues only if p99 tick time stays under the 33.3 ms budget at tick_rate 30 and the desync counter stays at zero. Then partition is set to 0 and the remaining pods update one at a time. Each pod gets a preStop hook that calls the drain endpoint on TCP 8080, which stops new party_slot assignments and signals session_reaper to skip sessions that are still live. terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 120, so sessions finish before the pod exits. ember-shard-us2 is updated only after ember-shard-eu1 is fully rolled. A rollback uses kubectl rollout undo statefulset/emberhold-shard in the production namespace, and the previous image tag is kept in the release notes. Hot reload of loot_table is not part of this flow; table changes ship as a new image.
As of 2 October 2026 snapshot_delta position fields use a bit-packed layout, replacing the 12 July 2026 decision to keep plain Protobuf; encode time reached 17% of tick budget.

Trap: the baseline_file silently stopped suppressing findings after a rule_pack upgrade on 22 July 2026. The baseline stores each finding keyed by rule id plus line number, so when rules-registry shipped rule_pack aws-core 2.4.0, which renamed 11 rule ids (for example aws-s3-001 became aws-s3-public-acl), every old entry stopped matching. The CI run on pebble-ci-runner then reported 143 new findings on a repository that had been clean the day before, and the job failed on severity_level error. Evidence: diffing .pebblelint-baseline.json against the sarif_output showed the same file paths and messages under new rule ids. Time lost: about half a day, spent first on suspecting the ast_walker cache. What to do instead: before bumping any rule_pack version, read the rename table in the rule_pack CHANGELOG and run `pebblelint baseline migrate --from 2.3.0 --to 2.4.0`, which rewrites ids in place. Pin rule_pack versions in pebblelint.config.json rather than using a caret range. Regenerate the baseline only as a last resort, because that hides real regressions. Reverses if the baseline key is changed to a content hash of the finding instead of rule id plus line, which is tracked as a future change.

The rules-registry host serves rule_pack tarballs over HTTPS on port 443 from the path /v1/packs/<name>/<version>.tgz. It sits behind a CDN with a 10 minute cache TTL. Publishing runs from the pebble-ci-runner job `publish-pack`, triggered by a git tag matching pack-*. The upload credential lives in 1Password under the entry for rules-registry publisher. Since 15 June 2026 the registry has been the only default source for packs.

Trap: the single-binary build crashed at startup on Node 20 runners on 9 August 2026 with 'WebAssembly.instantiate(): expected magic word' from the rules engine. Cause: the esbuild config inlined the .wasm file through the text loader, which decoded the bytes as UTF-8 and corrupted any byte above 0x7f. Local builds worked because they used a dev path that read engine.wasm from disk at runtime. Evidence: the bundle size was 212 KB smaller than the file size of engine.wasm plus the JS, and a hex dump of the embedded string began with ef bf bd replacement characters instead of 00 61 73 6d. The failure showed up only in the release artifact built on pebble-ci-runner, so unit tests passed. Time lost: about four hours. What to do instead: load the engine with esbuild's `binary` loader (or `base64` loader) in build/esbuild.config.ts, and keep the smoke test `scripts/smoke-binary.sh` in the release pipeline, which runs the packaged binary against fixtures/basic.tf and asserts exit code 1 with 3 findings. Never test only the dev entry point before tagging a release on any release_channel. Reverses if the engine is moved to a separate file shipped beside the binary.

Standing rule from Marisol Thandeka Verhoeven, stated 11 July 2026: no rule may ship as severity_level error in its first release. Every new rule starts at warn for one full minor release, then moves to error only after it has run on the open-source corpus of at least 200 public repositories with a false positive rate under 2 percent. Reason: the community adopted the tool on CI pipelines that fail on error, and a noisy new rule on a patch upgrade breaks builds for people who never opted in, which costs trust faster than a missed finding does. Rules that detect leaked secrets or public network exposure are the one exception and may start at error, but each exception needs a written note in the rule_pack CHANGELOG naming the reason. The promotion from warn to error is announced in the release notes for the release_channel stable, and never on the nightly channel alone. Reverses only if the project adds an opt-in strict mode that lets users choose to fail on new rules, in which case new rules could start at error under that mode only.

Convention for every repository, in force from 1 July 2026: configuration follows one layout so any host can be understood without reading the code.
